content: Sleight of Mouth is a structured system of linguistic techniques designed to influence and persuade others. This concept was developed by Robert Dilts, who analyzed and modeled the persuasive and argumentative skills of Richard Bandler, one of the co-founders of Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP). By deconstructing these methods, Dilts identified 14 foundational patterns of persuasion. Other contributors, such as Steve and Connirae Andreas, have expanded upon these original patterns by adding additional techniques. The purpose of formalizing these patterns, as with other aspects of NLP, is to enable individuals to understand the mechanisms of influence and to replicate these skills by applying one or more of the Sleight of Mouth patterns. The term Sleight of Mouth is a play on the phrase Sleight of Hand, which refers to a magician's ability to create seemingly impossible effects. The primary focus of Sleight of Mouth is to influence others by challenging and altering their beliefs. In this context, a belief is not merely a personal conviction, such as I believe in God, but rather a structured concept that can be analyzed and influenced. Two key types of beliefs are defined within this framework: 1. Complex Equivalence: This occurs when one thing is equated with another, such as X = Y or X is equivalent to Y. 2. Cause-Effect: This involves a causal relationship, where X causes Y or X results in Y. For example: A statement like You're late again, which means you don't love me demonstrates Complex Equivalence. Here, the speaker equates being late with a lack of love. A statement like I am not going to do that—I am not that kind of person. reflects a Cause-Effect belief, where the speaker implies that their identity determines their actions. Patterns of Sleight of Mouth The system includes a variety of patterns that can be used to challenge and reshape beliefs. Below is a detailed explanation of these patterns: 1. Intent: Focus on the underlying intention behind the belief. This can involve highlighting a positive intent or questioning a negative one. 2. Consequences: Identify a consequence of the belief, even if unintended, to challenge its validity. 3. Another Outcome: Suggest an alternative perspective or outcome that reframes the belief. 4. Counterexample: Provide an exception to the belief, thereby questioning its universality. 5. Apply to Self: Reflect the belief back onto the person making the statement, implying that it applies to them as well. 6. Reality Strategy: Challenge the belief by questioning the evidence or reasoning behind it. This involves asking how the person knows their belief is true or what specific aspects of the belief are problematic. 7. Model of the World: Argue that the belief is a metaphor for something else, rather than a literal truth. 8. Meta Frame: Challenge the foundational assumption behind the belief, suggesting that it presupposes something that may not be valid. 9. Change Frame Size: Broaden or narrow the scope of the belief by extending its implications to a larger or smaller scale, or over a longer or shorter time frame. 10. Hierarchy of Criteria: Question the belief by appealing to higher or more important values or criteria. 11. Chunk Down: Focus on a specific detail of the belief to challenge its validity. 12. Chunk Up: Generalize the belief to a broader context to expose its limitations. 13. Metaphor/Analogy: Use a metaphor or analogy to illustrate why the belief may not hold true. 14. Redefine: Reframe the belief using similar language but alter its implications. Examples of Application Here are examples of how these patterns can be applied to specific statements: Example 1: You're late again, which means you don't love me. Intent: I'm glad you care enough about me to be concerned about that. Consequence: You're just trying to get me to always fit within your timetable. Another Outcome: Would you have preferred me to cancel our dinner if I knew I was going to be late? Counterexample: Have you ever loved someone but still been late? Apply to Self: An accusation like that makes it sound like you don't love me. Reality Strategy: How did you come to that conclusion? Has someone accused you of something similar in the past? Model of the World: I'm guessing that it's not so much that I'm late, but you're concerned about me not focusing on the little things in our relationship. Meta Frame: Where did you learn that being on time equates to love? Change Frame Size: Most people are late for meetings every day—are you saying that none of them care? Hierarchy of Criteria: Isn't it more important that I actually made the effort to get here, in spite of everything that happened along the way? Chunk Down: What about all the times I have been on time? Chunk Up: You're judging an entire relationship based on time-keeping? Metaphor/Analogy: Isn't that like saying if you don't cook for me every time, you don't love me? Redefine: You're saying a small delay defines an entire relationship? Example 2: I am not going to do that—I am not that kind of person. Intent: It's great that you make decisions based on how you see yourself as a person. Consequence: Why are you focused on decisions that avoid you having to leave the house? Another Outcome: But if you don't do that, can you ever hope to develop into the person you'd like to become? Counterexample: Have you ever done something that you didn't think was 'you,' yet you really enjoyed it? Apply to Self: You're not the kind of person to pre-judge, yet here you are—pre-judging. Reality Strategy: And exactly what kind of person do you have to be to do that kind of thing? Model of the World: Does everyone who is afraid to try something new say that? Meta Frame: You're only saying that because you're afraid of what others might think. Change Frame Size: Yeah, that's right. Only a truly open-minded person would do that. Hierarchy of Criteria: What's more important—trying new things and expanding your horizons, or being safe and restricted in your tiny comfort zone? Chunk Down: What kind of person would that make you, specifically? Chunk Up: Do you always get out of trying new things by making excuses? Metaphor/Analogy: People aren't born astronauts. Redefine: You don't have to tie up your identity with a few actions. References Dilts, Robert (1999). Sleight of Mouth: The Magic of Conversational Belief Change. ISBN 0-916990-43-5. Andreas, Connirae (1992). Advanced Language Patterns.
